Lithium Therapy

which complication, and what to doIs this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech raised level toxicity: stop lithium IV isotonic fluids; escalate to hemodialysis for altered mental status, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia, or a level over 5.0, over 4.0 with impaired kidneys, or over 2.5 with prominent signs
  • High sodium dilute urine after years of use nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: restore volume; stop lithium if possible
  • High TSH low free thyroxine add levothyroxine; keep lithium going
What it is

Mood stabilizer; a first-line drug for bipolar mania and maintenance

Mechanism

Handled like sodium; the kidney is its only real exit

Thiazide, NSAID, ACE inhibitor or ARB more lithium reabsorbed level rises

Narrow therapeutic range

How lithium stabilizes mood is still not fully understood

Used for

Acute mania: first line, alone or with an antipsychotic

Bipolar maintenance (linked to lower suicide risk) bipolar I depression, both first line

Unipolar depression: add-on to an antidepressant, never alone

Risks

Toxicity nephrogenic diabetes insipidus hypothyroidism Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy (LMNOP)

Insights

Collecting duct: lithium blocks the cAMP signal of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) fewer aquaporins desmopressin barely changes the urine

Lithium enters collecting-duct cells through the epithelial sodium channel; amiloride blocks that entry, so it can treat the diabetes insipidus when lithium must continue

Diabetes insipidus dehydrates the level climbs: one complication feeds toxicity

Adverse effects, by systemroutine effects and complications
Nervous systemFine tremor is routine; coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia or drowsiness suggest toxicity; seizures and worsening mental status when severeRare complicationSILENT (syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity): permanent neurologic damage after lithium, mostly cerebellar, even without toxic levels
GutMetallic taste and diarrhea are common; nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are often the earliest signs of acute toxicity
KidneyPolyuria and thirst are common; about 20% of long-term users develop polyuria from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; kidney injury; prolonged use is linked to chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy
ThyroidLithium collects in the thyroid and slows hormone synthesis and release; goiter possibleHypothyroidism may develop in about 25% (quoted up to 50%), usually within 1 to 2 years of starting
HeartIn toxicity: bradycardia, atrioventricular block, T-wave flattening, QT (Q wave to T wave) interval prolongation
CalciumLong-term use is linked to persistent hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia; calcium yearly, PTH (parathyroid hormone) if high
PregnancyFirst-trimester exposure: Ebstein anomaly (see Urgent risks)
2Urgent risks
ToxicityLithium toxicity: findings commonly appear above 1.5 mmol/L
Acute: a recent large ingestion; nausea, vomiting, diarrhea often first Chronic: a long-term user; neurologic findings, even at lower levels

If lithium toxicity (a raised level) brings altered mental status, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia, choose hemodialysis, whatever the level.

LevelLevel over 5.0 mmol/L; over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function (creatinine over 2.0 mg/dL); or over 2.5 mmol/L with prominent signs of toxicity
In practice:Toxicology guidance recommends extracorporeal treatment above 4.0 mmol/L only when kidney function is impaired, and only suggests it above 5.0 mmol/L; hemodialysis is the preferred method

If any one of these is present, choose hemodialysis.

IngestionRecent large ingestion; alert, kidneys working, level under 2.5 mmol/L
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium

If no dialysis criterion is met, choose IV isotonic fluids and serial levels.

Water lossDrowsy and volume-depleted with diabetes insipidus
Dehydration also raises the lithium level

If sodium is high and the urine dilute, choose volume replacement and a lithium level.

PregnancyFirst-trimester exposure: more cardiac malformations, mainly Ebstein anomaly
Breastfeeding on lithium is not advisable

If exposure fell in the first trimester, choose fetal echocardiography.

3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
Thirst, polyuria; confusion with dehydrationYears of use; high sodium with dilute urine; little or no desmopressin response
Tiredness, cold intolerance, mental fogginess; may have a goiterUsually within 1 to 2 years; high TSH with low free thyroxine, or a TSH over 10 μU/mL
Routine side effectsFine tremor, polyuria, metallic taste, mildly high TSHSodium, mental status, level and free thyroxine all normal
Chronic toxicityLong-term user; new thiazide, NSAID, ACE inhibitor or ARB, or dehydrationNeurologic findings lead; raised level (after a thiazide it usually rises within 10 days)
Acute toxicityRecent large ingestionSoon after ingestion: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea often come first; raised level
Obesity with polyuria suggests glucose diuresisGlucose high; urine not dilute (solute diuresis)
Primary polydipsiaPolyuria with dilute urine; especially common in psychiatric patientsSodium low, not high; urine concentrates above 600 mOsm/kg after water deprivation
Polyuria with dilute urineDesmopressin clearly raises urine osmolality
Hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemiaRaised calcium on routine labsYears of lithium; calcium high on the yearly check; measure PTH
LMNOP
  • L – lithium
  • M – movement: tremor
  • N – nephrology: kidney injury and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (thirst, heavy urination)
  • O – hypothyroidism
  • P – pregnancy: Ebstein's anomaly
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Thirst and polyuria plus confusionWater loss, not the routine polyuriaSodium with urine osmolality
A new thiazide, NSAID, ACE inhibitor or ARBA rising levelLevel and creatinine
Mildly high TSH beside a high sodium and dilute urineA decoy: the thyroid explains neitherRead the sodium against the urine; add free thyroxine
Bradycardia on lithiumToxicity possibleECG and a level
No tremor or nystagmusAgainst chronic toxicity; acute toxicity can start with gut symptoms onlyCheck a level anyway

Pause point. The bait: a mildly raised TSH offered as hypothyroidism, or confusion offered as acute toxicity. Hypernatremia with dilute urine after years of use belongs to the kidney, and the thyroid explains neither lab; acute toxicity needs a large ingestion. The water loss can still push the level up, so check one.

7Treatment
1

1st linetoxicity with nausea, diarrhea, a coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech or an unsteady gait; mental status intact, no dialysis criterion met

Stop lithium; IV isotonic fluids; serial levels

In practice:For mild toxicity, stopping lithium alone may be enough Charcoal does not bind lithium. Guideline detailGastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation may be considered, mainly for sustained-release tablets; charcoal only for a suspected coingestion Guideline detailEvery 2 to 4 hours during treatment; sustained-release tablets peak later (about 4 to 5 hours), so repeat the level

2

Escalatealtered mental status, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia; or a level over 5.0 mmol/L, over 4.0 with impaired kidneys, or over 2.5 with prominent signs

Hemodialysis
Manage by effect
EffectDoAvoid
ToxicityStop lithium; IV isotonic fluids; dialysis by the criteria aboveActivated charcoal: it does not bind lithium
Diabetes insipidus, drowsy and volume-depletedReplace volume first; check the levelDesmopressin: little or no effect
Stop lithium if possible, then restrict salt; if lithium must continue, add amiloride (salt restriction would raise the level); keep free water available; a low-protein diet cuts the solute loadA thiazide or NSAID without close levels: both raise the lithium level
HypothyroidismAdd levothyroxine; continue lithiumStopping lithium: thyroid changes are not a reason
Routine thyroid changeContinue lithium; recheck TSH in 4 to 6 monthsStopping lithium
Infection, heavy sweating or diarrheaConsider a lower dose; watch for dehydrationStarting a thiazide, NSAID, ACE inhibitor or ARB without a level check
8Follow-up
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Before startingCreatinine, BUN (blood urea nitrogen), TSH, calcium with albumin; weight, height, blood pressure; a pregnancy test if pregnancy is possible Guideline detailWith cardiac disease or cardiac risk factors, or in older adults, add an ECG before startingBaselines for the kidney, thyroid and calcium effects, and the teratogenic risk
After startingLevel at 7 days, then every 1 to 2 weeks until two in a row are in range at one doseNarrow range: the dose is titrated to the level
Every 6 to 12 monthsLevel, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, TSHKidney and thyroid effects build over years
YearlyCalcium with albumin; PTH if calcium is highLong-term use is linked to hyperparathyroidism
Raised TSH, normal free thyroxineRecheck in 4 to 6 months; levothyroxine once free thyroxine falls or TSH passes 10 μU/mL, or a trial if symptoms appearThyroid changes build over time; they are not a reason to stop lithium

Levels are troughs, drawn about 12 hours after the last dose. Targets: acute mania 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L (= mEq/L) under age 65; maintenance 0.6 to 1.0 (some sources use 0.8 as the floor); toxic above 1.5.

Interactions
WithEffectDo
Thiazide diureticLevel usually rises within 10 days; size of the rise unpredictable Guideline detailThiazides raise lithium far more than loop diuretics doLevel and creatinine more often
NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug)Raises the level (more is reabsorbed); case reports range from about 10% to over 400%Level and creatinine more often
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker)Raises the levelLevel and kidney function more often
MetronidazoleCan raise the levelCheck the level
Acetazolamide, urea, xanthine preparations, alkalinizing agentsLower the level: more lithium leaves in the urineCheck the level
Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, low-sodium dietRaise the levelCheck the level; consider a lower dose
Practice
  1. 59-year-old man with bipolar disorder, on lithium 8 years lisinopril started 2 weeks ago 4 days of nausea and a coarse tremor of both hands alert and oriented HR 64/min · BP 126/80 mm Hg · sodium 139 mEq/L → Serum lithium level and creatinine → an ACE inhibitor raises the lithium level; coarse tremor and nausea suggest toxicity
  2. 44-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable lithium 6 years 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea drowsy; oriented to person only coarse tremor, slurred speech, unsteady gait HR 56/min · sodium 138 mEq/L · creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) · urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg → Chronic lithium toxicity → dehydration raised the level in a long-term user, and neurologic findings lead; a serum lithium level confirms
  3. 22-year-old woman took 30 immediate-release lithium tablets 2 hours ago started lithium 3 weeks ago vomited 3 times; diarrhea alert, oriented; no tremor HR 96/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg · lithium 2.2 mmol/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → IV isotonic fluids and serial lithium levels → alert, kidneys working and level under 2.5 mmol/L: no dialysis criterion is met; lithium does not bind charcoal
  4. 67-year-old man on lithium for 15 years a week of poor intake; took extra tablets yesterday drowsy, confused; responds only to a loud voice coarse tremor HR 54/min · BP 100/62 mm Hg · lithium 4.4 mmol/L · creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.1) → Urgent hemodialysis → decreased consciousness, or a level over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidneys: either one indicates dialysis; lithium does not bind charcoal
  5. 62-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable lithium dose for 9 years hydrochlorothiazide started for hypertension 3 weeks ago now coarse tremor, slurred speech, confusion HR 60/min · lithium 2.4 mmol/L · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Increased renal reabsorption of lithium → a thiazide increases renal reabsorption of lithium, which is handled like sodium; the kidney is its only real exit
  6. 54-year-old man on lithium for 10 years for bipolar disorder knee osteoarthritis pain; asks what to take for it euthymic, alert and oriented BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Oral naproxen, taken daily → NSAIDs raise the lithium level
  7. 46-year-old man on lithium for 14 years 6 months of thirst passing large volumes of urine day and night euthymic, alert and oriented BP 124/78 mm Hg · sodium 146 mEq/L · glucose 94 mg/dL · urine osmolality 160 mOsm/kg → Collecting duct unresponsive to antidiuretic hormone → lithium blocks the ADH (antidiuretic hormone) signal, so fewer aquaporins reach the membrane; desmopressin changes the urine little or not at all
  8. 58-year-old woman on lithium for 16 years months of thirst and polyuria in bed 2 days after a fall now drowsy and disoriented HR 104/min · BP 102/64 mm Hg · sodium 156 mEq/L · urine osmolality 140 mOsm/kg · creatinine 1.3 mg/dL → IV fluid replacement and a serum lithium level → water and volume loss from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; dehydration also raises the lithium level; the drowsiness fits a sodium of 156, and the level is not yet known, so replace volume and measure it
  9. 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 18 months 2 months of tiredness and feeling cold small nontender goiter alert and oriented HR 62/min · TSH 12.4 μU/mL · free thyroxine low · sodium 140 mEq/L · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Add levothyroxine and continue lithium → lithium-induced hypothyroidism; thyroid abnormalities are not a reason to stop lithium
  10. 26-year-old man, lithium for 4 months; euthymic mild tremor holding a cup urinating more than before alert, oriented, gait normal HR 72/min · sodium 140 mEq/L · urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg · TSH 5.6 μU/mL · free thyroxine normal · trough 0.9 mmol/L → Expected lithium adverse effects → normal sodium, mental status, level and free thyroxine; a fine tremor, polyuria and a mildly high TSH are routine
  11. 40-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 3 years takes no other medications routine visit; last laboratory studies 12 months ago alert and oriented BP 118/74 mm Hg · BMI (body mass index) 23 kg/m² → Lithium level, creatinine, TSH and calcium → level, electrolytes, creatinine and TSH every 6 to 12 months; calcium yearly
How NBME framed it: question 1

50-year-old woman brought to the emergency department: trouble speaking, cannot walk mildly agitated, uncooperative, not oriented to place Husband: lithium for 20 years for bipolar disorder; lately more thirst and urination No family history of kidney or endocrine disease 163 cm, 77 kg, BMI 29 kg/m² · T 36.8 °C · pulse 84/min · BP 110/75 mm Hg · speech difficulty, muscle weakness, the cognitive findings; otherwise normal · sodium 150 mEq/L · TSH 5.5 μU/mL · urine specific gravity 1.005 · urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg

Most likely cause of her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Acute lithium toxicity: confusion and trouble walking fit toxicity; but acute toxicity follows a large ingestion, and the labs here point to the kidney.
  • Lithium-induced hypothyroidism: the TSH of 5.5 is mildly high; but no free thyroxine is given, and hypothyroidism explains neither the hypernatremia nor the dilute urine.
  • Routine side effects of lithium: polyuria alone is routine; but dehydration, confusion, hypernatremia and dilute urine can be life-threatening.
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus: a BMI of 29 with polyuria suggests glucose diuresis; but hypernatremia after years of lithium fits the kidney better.

Down to two: lithium-induced diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. Diabetes insipidus: 20 years of lithium, thirst and polyuria, then a sodium of 150 with urine osmolality 200; the kidney is losing water it should keep. The stem never names diabetes insipidus or gives a lithium level, so the answer rests on reading the sodium against the urine. Four of the five options are lithium effects, and the one lab placed to tempt, a mildly high TSH, belongs to the wrong one.

Pairs with Polyuria: the renal workup of a dilute urine and the agent used when lithium must continue. Teratogenic Exposures: lithium in pregnancy. Thyroid Disease in an Adult: reading the TSH.
Transferable rule

When a patient on a drug with several known complications presents, choose the complication that explains every abnormal value. On lithium, a high sodium with dilute urine belongs to the kidney, and a mildly high TSH beside it is not the answer.
